:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1997)
tamagotchi_pets <- tibble(
  pet_id = 1:450,
  care = rep(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), each = 150)) |>
  mutate(care = factor(care, levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")),
         lifespan_days = round(rweibull(n(), shape = 2.2,
           scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13,
                     Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)]), 1))
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans (simulated)",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
  labs_ovrlp_hist
```

## Description

Overlapping histograms allow us to compare distributions across the groups of a categorical (or ordinal) variable.

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::


Install packages.


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

In 1997, kids everywhere were feeding, cleaning, and playing with Tamagotchis, and how long a virtual pet lived depended on how well it was cared for. We'll simulate the lifespans of 450 pets, 150 for each level of care. `rweibull()` draws each lifespan from a Weibull distribution, and the `scale` for each level of care (6, 13, or 21 days) stretches the lifespans of better cared for pets. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 450 pets every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1997)
tamagotchi_pets <- tibble(
  pet_id = 1:450,
  care = rep(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), each = 150)) |>
  mutate(care = factor(care, levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")),
         lifespan_days = round(rweibull(n(), shape = 2.2,
           scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13,
                     Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)]), 1))
glimpse(tamagotchi_pets)
```
:::

## Distribution

Overlapping histograms compare the shape of one variable across groups. Here the groups have the same *kind* of shape (they all come from the same distribution), but each one is stretched by a different amount. Below we'll move from the pets, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first five pets (all neglected).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(tamagotchi_pets, 5)
```
:::

None of these neglected pets made it past nine days. The summary below compares the three levels of care. Each mean is a little higher than its median, and the longest lived pet in each group lasted more than twice as long as the median.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
tamagotchi_pets |> 
  group_by(care) |> 
  summarise(
    mean = mean(lifespan_days), 
    median = median(lifespan_days), 
    max = max(lifespan_days))
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The histograms below are drawn on top of each other (`position = "identity"`), and the lines are the Weibull curves we drew the lifespans from, scaled to match the counts. Every group has the same lopsided hump with a tail to the right. Better care doesn't change the shape; it stretches the hump to the right and flattens it out.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
weibull_curves <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  care = factor(c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered"), 
    levels = c("Neglected", "Average", "Pampered")),
  lifespan_days = seq(0, 45, by = 0.25)) |> 
  mutate(scale = c(Neglected = 6, Average = 13, 
                   Pampered = 21)[as.character(care)],
         count = 150 * (45 / 40) * dweibull(lifespan_days, 
           shape = 2.2, scale = scale))

ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets, aes(x = lifespan_days, fill = care)) + 
  geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", 
    binwidth = 45 / 40, boundary = 0) + 
  geom_line(data = weibull_curves, aes(y = count, color = care), 
    linewidth = 1, show.legend = FALSE) + 
  labs(x = "Lifespan (days)", y = "Pets", fill = "Care")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The [Weibull distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weibull_distribution) is a common model for lifetimes. It has a shape ($k$) and a scale ($\lambda$):

$$
X \sim \text{Weibull}(k = 2.2, \; \lambda_{\text{care}}), \quad \lambda = (6, 13, 21)
$$

The chance that a pet is still alive after $t$ days is $e^{-(t/\lambda)^k}$. When the shape is greater than 1 (like our 2.2), the risk of a pet dying grows the longer it lives, which gives the histogram its hump and right tail. The scale stretches everything: the median lifespan is $\lambda (\ln 2)^{1/k}$, which is about 5, 11, and 18 days for our three groups. Our simulated medians are `r paste(round(tapply(tamagotchi_pets$lifespan_days, tamagotchi_pets$care, median), 1), collapse = ", ")` days. 

Try changing `shape` in `rweibull()`. A shape of 1 turns the hump into a steady decline (pets die at the same rate no matter their age), and a large shape makes every pet in a group die at about the same time.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::


  -   Create labels with `labs()`

  -   Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  -   Map `lifespan_days` to the `x` axis and `care` to `fill`

  -   Inside `geom_histogram()`, set `alpha` to `2/3`, `position` to `"identity"` (so the bars overlap instead of stacking), and `bins` to `40`

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_ovrlp_hist
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans (simulated)",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
  labs_ovrlp_hist
```
:::



::: {.column-margin}
Experiment with different `binwidth`s when comparing distributions across groups.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

Histograms work by dividing the variable provided to `x` [*into bins and counting the number of observations in each bin.*](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_histogram.html)

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
```{r}
#| label: create_graph_ovrlp_hist
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_ovrlp_hist <- labs(
  title = "Tamagotchi lifespans (simulated)",
  subtitle = "450 virtual pets and how they were cared for",
  x = "Lifespan (days)",
  fill = "Care")
ggp2_ovrlp_hist <- ggplot(data = tamagotchi_pets,
     aes(x = lifespan_days,
         fill = care)) +
     geom_histogram(alpha = 2/3, position = "identity", bins = 40)
ggp2_ovrlp_hist +
  labs_ovrlp_hist
```
:::
